analytic.title: Time-Triggered Scheduling for Time-Sensitive Networking with Preemption

div.p: Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) is a set of IEEE 802.1 technologies that support real-time and reliable Ethernet communication, commonly used in automotive and industrial automation systems. Time-aware scheduling is adopted in TSN to achieve high temporal predictability. In this paper, we demonstrate that such a scheduling solution alone does not always meet all timing requirements and must be combined with network preemption support. We propose an SMT-based synthesis method for preemptive time-triggered scheduling and routing in TSN. Our experiments demonstrate that schedulability is improved significantly when using frame preemption compared to a standard time-triggered message scheduling approach.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: The use of Ethernet in many embedded and cyber-physical systems is growing rapidly, due to ever increasing requirements on communication bandwidth. Several examples can be found in the automotive sector, in particular in the development of advanced driver assistance and driving automation systems. Other examples can be found in the avionics and telecommunications industries. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) technology has been developed recently by the IEEE 802.1 standardization group to enhance switched Ethernet technology with real-time and dependability capabilities. Examples include time-synchronization protocols [7], enhancements for scheduled time-triggered traffic [10], and solutions for redundant frame transmission [9]. Time-triggered scheduling is widely adopted in safety-critical systems at the processor [20] and network level [3], [18], [21], [22] due to its high predictability capabilities [11], [12]. However, for applications with tight real-time constraints, it is not always possible to find a timetriggered schedule that meets all deadlines.

Contribution: To improve schedulability for time-triggered scheduling, we propose its combined use with frame preemption (802.1Qbu) [8], which was introduced recently in TSN to add flexibility in the temporal domain. By using the recently introduced preemption capability by TSN, we combine flexibility with the typical high predictability associated with time-triggered communication scheduling. As we demonstrate in this paper, this combination often makes the difference in tightly time-constrained applications being schedulable. We offer an SMT-based approach that is effective and efficient in scheduling a TSN network with time-triggered communication and preemption. Our solution provides time-triggered schedules of all messages, involving statically scheduling their preemption points, as well as allocation of messages to the preemptable and express MAC interfaces across all ports in the network. In addition to these contributions, we make several efforts to ensure practical relevance: our SMT formulation includes routing constraints, allowing the solver to optimize message routes, in addition to the communication schedules; and our solution considers overheads associated with frame preemption per the IEEE TSN preemption standard as well as networks for which not all switches and ports have hardware support for preemption at the MAC layer.

Related Work: Pioneering work by Steiner [18] and Craciunas et al. [3] includes SMT-based techniques to synthesize time-triggered schedules for Ethernet networks. Several researchers have addressed integrated routing and time-triggered scheduling for real-time and control applications [6], [13], [17]. Zhou et al. [21], [22] further considered reliability aspects in TSN networks. However, none of the aforementioned solutions consider preemption on the network.

Thiele and Ernst [19] proposed an analysis method to calculate worst-case latencies under preemptive scheduling in TSN. Lo Bello et al. [2] extended the analysis with preemptive credit-based shaping and time-aware shaping. Park et al. [16] considered fixed-priority preemptive scheduling in TSN, where the priority of each message and the assignment of messages to eMAC or pMAC egress is determined. Finally, researchers have also presented new preemption models, which are not supported and in compliance with the TSN standard: Ojewale et al. [14], [15] proposed a multi-level preemption solution and Ashjaei et al. [1] a new preemption model, where the timeaware and crebit-based shapers are considered jointly. None of the above results, however, is relevant in the context of time-triggered scheduling.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: The network topology is modeled as a graph G(V, E), where a node v i ∈ V is a network switch or an end system, and an edge [v i , v j ] is a full-duplex link that allows simultaneous communication between two nodes in both directions. A switch has multiple ports, each comprising an ingress portion for incoming messages and an egress portion for outgoing messages. Fig. 3 shows an example of network topology with 3 switches (i.e., v 2 , v 3 , and v 4 ) and 3 end systems (i.e., v 1 , v 5 , and v 6 ).

The switch architecture is shown in Fig. 1, focusing on the ingress portion of Port A and the egress portion of Port B, with hardware support for frame preemption. An incoming message arrives at an ingress port (Port A in the example) and goes through a forwarding engine and dispatcher that, based on an address resolution logic (ARL) table (also called forwarding table), determines the egress port and the corresponding queue on which to queue the message for forwarding throughout the network. The forwarding process incurs a delay (forwarding delay), which is the time from receiving a message to putting it into the corresponding egress queue. For a port that supports frame preemption, the MAC service interface of the egress port can be divided into two categories: the eMAC interface (for express traffic) and the pMAC interface (for preemptable traffic). Messages that are assigned to the eMAC and the pMAC interfaces, respectively, are called eMAC messages and pMAC messages. Only an eMAC message can preempt a pMAC message that is currently in transmission on the link. Messages in the same category cannot preempt each other. Thus, there is only one level of preemption in TSN. We consider that it is given whether or not a given port of a given switch supports frame preemption.

Format of pMAC frame: At the sender side, due to the preemption, a message can be transmitted as several segments, each with different formats. The format of each segment is shown in Fig. 2, where the left side of the arrow is the original pMAC frame and this can be transmitted as three segments and the format of these three are shown, for example, in the right side of the arrow. The size of the header for the first segment are different from the intermediate and last segments and their transmission time are denoted as ζ ij and ρ ij , respectively, as transmitted on link [v i , v j ]. The minimum size requirement μ for each segment should be satisfied. At the receiver side, all segments of a message can be detected and they will be assembled as a single pMAC frame according to the format shown in the left side of the arrow.

A message m i has a source v i.src and destination v i.dest . End systems in the network act as sources or destinations for messages. Message m i is generated periodically with period P i and has a relative end-to-end deadline e2e i . During the offline scheduling, for a certain message m i , schedules of several message instances m ij need to be determined for one hyper-period. We denote by m ij the j th instance of m i . div.head: III. MOTIVATIONAL EXAMPLE
div.p: Let us consider the example network topology in Fig. 3 and a set of messages with parameters shown in Table I. A nonpreemptive TSN schedule of these messages is shown in Fig 4 . The figure shows the schedule of all message transmissions across all links in the network, for one hyper-period. As can be seen by the schedule for link [v 4 , v 5 ], the deadline constraint for the second instance of message m 1 cannot be satisfied due to the long transmission times of message m 2 .

Let us now consider that all switches on the network support frame preemption and message m 1 is assigned to the eMAC interface on all egress ports along its route to the destination, and message m 2 is assigned to the pMAC interface on all egress ports. Fig. 5 shows a schedule that meets all deadline constraints by using preemption on the egress port of switch v 2 connected to v 3 . On this link, the second instance of m 1 preempts the transmission of the first instance of m 2 . The endto-end latency for the second instance of message m 1 has been reduced from 7 to 4 by the use of only one preemption, thus demonstrating the importance and efficiency of using frame preemption to make the entire system schedulable.

Note that we ignored the frame headers shown in Fig. 2 in this example for brevity of presentation. The problem statement, solution, and results included in this paper consider all transmission time overheads caused by the frame headers in preemptable messages.

div.p: The inputs to the problem solved in this paper are as follows:
• Network topology given by a graph G(V, E). • A flag kl that, if 1, indicates that the port connecting switches v k and v l supports preemption (and 0 id preemption is not supported).

• Schedule: Release time r ijl of each message instance m ij at each link (egressing from node v l ) along the route of the message. • Route: Destination nodes for messages on switches. The objective is to synthesize the routing and preemptive schedule such that the deadline constraint for each message is satisfied. Note that our approach actually determines the release time r k ijl of each segment k of a preemptable message through our exact model of frame preemption in the TSN standard.

V. APPROACH In this section, we first give an example on how to build the constraints for preemptive scheduling, and then we propose the Satisfiability Modulo Theories (SMT) formulation for TSN scheduling with preemptions.

div.head: A. Example of Preemption-Aware Scheduling Constraints
div.p: Let us now consider an example with two messages m 1 and m 2 , where m 1 is assigned to the eMAC interface, and m 2 to the pMAC interface. This means that m 1 can preempt m 2 . Both messages are transmitted from switch v 1 to v 2 . Let us consider a maximum number of segments λ = 3 for the pMAC message m 2 , for this example. This refers to the frame segments in Fig. 2 and we thus limit the number of preemptions of m 2 to maximal 2. In addition, to comply with the frame preemption standard in TSN as shown in Fig. 2, we denote by μ the minimum size requirement (translated to transmission time) for each segment. We shall now consider four different scenarios (A through D) in scheduling the communications of m 1 and m 2 .

In this case, m 2 is not preempted and it is transmitted as one segment. div.head: B. SMT Formulation of TSN Scheduling Constraints with Preemption
div.p: To prepare for the presentation of the general SMT formulation for TSN scheduling with preemption, we introduce the following generic notation: Considering a link [v k , v l ], the time overheads of the header of the first preemptable message segment and the second (and subsqeuent) message segment are denoted by ζ kl and ρ kl , respectively. The release and finish times of the k th segment of message instance m ij on node v l are denoted by r k ijl and f k ijl , respectively. To indicate whether a message m ij on switch v k is assigned to the eMAC interface or pMAC interface of the corresponding egress port along the message route, we introduce a flag κ ijk : The message is assigned to eMAC if κ ijk is 1, whereas the message is assigned to pMAC if κ ijk is 0 (the actual value of the flag κ ijk is determined by the solver as the part of the solution of the TSN formulation).
Let us now discuss the constraints for TSN scheduling with preemption:
• Constraint to model that messages belonging to the same category are contention free: If two messages are both assigned to the eMAC or pMAC egress, constraint (4) should be satisfied:

div.head: VI. HEURISTICS
div.p: Scheduling and routing synthesis for time-triggered messages using SMT is known to be NP-complete [18], and the problem complexity is further increased with the consideration of preemption. To improve the runtime scalability of our framework, we apply two incremental synthesis strategies for scheduling and routing with SMT.

In the first strategy, we divide the hyper-period into several stages, where the minimal size of a stage is the minimum message period. The algorithm solves several problems of smaller size in an incremental fashion. First, the messages instantiated inside the first stage are scheduled and routed, thus solving the SMT formulation for the decision variables corresponding to a subset of message instances. In subsequent steps, schedules and routes are synthesized iteratively by running the SMT solver for the decision variables corresponding to the messages instantiated in the time intervals corresponding to the successive stages, while the decision variables determined in the previous steps are fixed. In our second strategy, each stage is addressed in successive sub-steps. In each sub-step, a subset of the messages instantiated in the respective stage is scheduled/routed. Additional messages are considered sub-step by sub-step until all messages instantiated inside the respective stage have been scheduled, with the schedules from prior substeps provided as immutable inputs.

Such heuristics do not constitute a contribution of this paper and are considered state-of-the-art; their efficiency and effectiveness for time-triggered scheduling of packet-switched networks have been demonstrated by several research groups [13], [17], [18].

div.head: VII. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: In this section, we evaluate the efficiency of the proposed approach. All of the experiments are conducted on a desktop computer with a 3.40 GHz Core (TM) i7-3770 CPU and 8 GB of RAM, running an Ubuntu 16.04 operating system. The SMT solver we used to solve the synthesis problem is z3 [4], which is a state-of-the-art SMT solver. In our experiments, we consider all link speeds to be 100 Mbit/s and message sizes to be between 42 bytes and 1500 bytes. The periods for all messages range from 10 ms to 100 ms. We consider a network with 16 end systems and the number of switches between 4, 6, and 8. The network topology is generated randomly using the Erdos-Renyi graph model [5]. All points in the following diagrams represent the average result of 30 experiments. For these experiments, we applied incremental synthesis (see section VI). We divided the hyperperiod into the maximum number of stages (each stage has the size of the minimum message period) and we consider the maximum number of sub-steps in each stage (corresponding to one additional message per sub-step).

div.head: A. Scaling
div.p: In this section, we explore the scaling of the proposed approach as the number of switches, preemptions and message instances increases.

In the first set of experiments, we fix the number of message instances to be 50 and evaluate the impact of increasing number of switches and number of maximal segments (i.e., number of preemptions) on the synthesis time. The number of switches between 4, 6, 8 and the number of segments varies from 1 to 13. The experimental results are shown in Fig 9 . It is not unexpected that the synthesis time increases with the number of switches as well as with the maximum number of segments. However, it is important to observe that up to a maximum number of 7 segments, this increase is modest and synthesis times are low. The increase of the synthesis time becomes significant only beyond a maximum number of 7 segments. This observation is important in the context of our experiments regarding schedulability discussed in the next subsection.

In the second set of experiments, we fix the number of switches to be 8 and evaluate the impact of increasing number of message instances and number of maximal segments on the synthesis time. The experimental results are shown in Fig. 10 and11. The synthesis time increases, of course, with the number of message instances and with the maximum number of segments but, as observed also in the previous experiment (Fig. 9), the increase becomes significant only beyond a maximum number of 7 segments.

div.head: B. Schedulability
div.p: Given a certain set of messages, allowing for preemption is supposed to increase the likelihood of finding a schedulable solution (even in the context in which the overhead slightly increases due to preemption). We have performed a set of experiments in order to investigate this aspect. We considered cases with 50 and 134 message instances, respectively. The number of switches is 8. For each case we increased the maximum number of segments from 1 (no preemption) to 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11. For the 30 experiments run for each point we calculated the percentage of schedulable cases and the 3D-5

results are shown in Fig. 12. As expected, the percentage of schedulable solutions increases with the maximum allowed number of segments. Nevertheless, due to the parameters of the messages, their deadlines, and the features of the platform, there is a limit beyond which an increased amount of preemption will no longer affect schedulability. As observed in Fig. 12, this saturation point is around a maximum number of 7 preemptions. This is important for two reasons: (1) As shown in Fig. 9 and 10, the synthesis time is growing faster only beyond a maximum number of 7 segments. (2) The designer needs to explore only a very limited range for the input parameter λ (representing the maximum number of segments); one would start with a low value and increase λ if the solver does not return a schedulable solution; no solution for around 7 segments is an indication for the fact that the application is not schedulable.

div.head: C. Distribution of Number of Preemptions on the Network
div.p: Our next experiment does not explore the performance of the proposed solution but illustrates how the scheduler employs the opportunity of preemption in order to find a schedulable solution. We have run one test case with 50 message instances and 8 switches. We found a schedulable solution with a maximum number of 4 preemptions (5 segments). Fig. 13 shows the distribution of the number of preemptions as applied to the 50 messages. We can observe that 44% of the 50 message instances are not preempted, whereas 39% are preempted one time.

We now reduce all message deadlines by 18% and observe that our SMT tool cannot find a feasible solution with maximum number of preemptions equal to 4. We then increase the maximum number of preemptions to 6 and observe that we find a feasible solution with Fig. 14 showing the distribution of preemptions. Comparing Fig. 13 and Fig. 14, we conclude that, by reducing the deadlines, messages generally need more preemptions to meet the more stringent deadlines. We also note that, for both cases, the number of preemptions for the majority of the messages is 0 and 1.

div.head: D. Real-life Example
div.p: We finally applied our approach to a real-life example from General Motors. The example consists of 27 applications (including active safety, engine control, sensor fusion, semiautomated driving, surround view, maps, and vehicle location) that need to communicate by messages on TSN, with periods in the range of 20 to 100 ms, deadlines in the range of 2 to 10 ms, and message sizes in the range of 100 and 1500 bytes. These 27 applications generate 173 message instances within the hyper-period of 200 ms. The network consists of 8 switches. In the case of no preemptions, there is no solution that meets all deadlines. When we increase the number of preemptions for all messages to 1, we find a feasible solution in 22.47 seconds. This shows the efficiency of applying timetriggered scheduling with preemptions on practical real-life examples.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: We considered the synthesis of preemptive time-triggered scheduling in Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN). Scheduling and routing constraints, as well as efficient heuristics, are proposed to perform the synthesis of preemptive time-triggered scheduling in TSN. Several experiments are conducted to demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed approach in improving schedulability.
